en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk (Kosiyavagga) 20.
The Training Rule on Buying and Selling (Kayavikkaya-sikkhāpada).
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta was occupied with making robes.
Having made a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) from pieces of coarse cloth, and having dyed it well and finished it skillfully, he put it on.
Then a certain wanderer, having put on a very expensive cloth, approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta:
“Friend, this outer robe of yours is beautiful;
give it to me in exchange for my upper garment.
“Know for yourself, friend,” he replied.
“Yes, friend, I know,” he replied.
“Well then, friend,” [the other said], and he gave it to him. Then that wanderer, having put on the outer robe, went to the wanderers’ park.
The wanderers said this to that wanderer:
"Friend, this outer robe of yours is beautiful;
where did you get it?"
“I have exchanged it for that cloth, friend.
“Friend, this outer robe of yours will last for many days;
that cloth of yours is the better bargain.”
Then that wanderer thought, “The wanderers have spoken the truth: ‘In how many days will this outer robe of mine be finished? This very cloth is better for me.
He approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son; having approached, he said to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, “Here, friend, is your outer robe; give me the cloth.”
“But did I not say to you, friend, ‘Find out, friend’?
I will not give it.
Then that wanderer complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“Even householders give to a householder who feels remorse;
how much more, then, would one who has gone forth not give to another who has gone forth?
The bhikkhus heard that wanderer reproaching, grumbling, and complaining.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta engage in buying and selling with a wanderer?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before].
“Is it true, Upananda, that you entered into a transaction involving buying and selling with a wanderer?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before] ...
"How indeed, foolish man, could you engage in buying and selling with a wanderer?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whatever monk should engage in various kinds of buying and selling, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
“Whatever monk” means whichever kind of monk... [and so on].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Of various kinds" means:
"Robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—even down to a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, or a thread for a fly-whisk.
"Should engage in buying and selling":
"Give this for that; bring that for this; exchange this for that; barter this for that. If he transgresses, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

When one's own goods have been bartered away and have come into the hands of another, and another's goods have been purchased and have come into one's own hands, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
… [as before] … “Venerable sir, I engaged in various kinds of buying and selling.
This is my article to be relinquished.”
“I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. … “One should give it” … “They should give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the venerable one.
If there is buying and selling, and he perceives it as buying and selling, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If there is buying and selling, but he is uncertain of it, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is not a sale of a human being, but one perceives it as such, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it is not a sale of a human being, but one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a sale of a human being, but one is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a purchase and sale, and he perceives it as a purchase and sale,
there is no offense. There is no offense when he asks for the price.
He points it out to the one who prepares what is allowable, saying, "This is ours; we have need of this and that," [if he is] insane.
"For the first offender":
thus ends the tenth training rule concerning buying and selling.
This concludes the second chapter on Silk.
Its summary verse:
Silk, two-and-a-half-fold [cloth],
and the sitting mat for six years.
And he should pluck out two hairs,
both of which are of different kinds.
